title: Living ashtpadi 9
hookLine: drop one title and keep the substance

lines: A FAMILY OF SINGHS AND KAURS.
cards: A Sikh family is introduced at a wedding. Harpreet Kaur, her husband Jaswant Singh, their son Arjun Singh, their daughter Simran Kaur, and the grandmother, also a Kaur.
Then the woman from another village who runs the langar kitchen: Kaur again. Elsewhere, a surname can tell a stranger your caste, your clan, your rank.
These two names are shared on purpose, and they tell the room nothing of the kind. That's ashtpadi nine, carried into everyday life.

teach.h: FOUR TITLES, EACH GIVEN A LIFE.
teach.b: Ashtpadi nine took the honored titles of its day, the aparas, the vaishnav, the bhagauti, the pandit, and poured a matching life into each one. Untouched by falsehood. Doing good, not gripped by reward.

Teaching your own mind first. Stanza after stanza: the name is nothing without the substance underneath it. Later, Sikh tradition remembers Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, making that idea visible.
Tradition says that when he founded the Khalsa, he gave the initiated men the name Singh, meaning lion, and the women the name Kaur, often explained as princess.

The same names for everyone, whatever family or caste they came from. Today some Sikhs use Singh or Kaur in place of a caste surname, and others carry them alongside a family name; there's real variety.
But the idea behind the custom is the one Guru Arjan was teaching in Sukhmani: titles that rank people don't decide who someone is. For any of us, living ashtpadi nine can be smaller than a new name.
It can be letting go of one title in your own head: the clever one, the responsible one, the one who's always right, the expert.

teach.h: DROP THE BADGE, KEEP THE WORK.
teach.b: Not the work behind it, just the label.
Keep the substance. Drop the badge.

how: Sikhs use the names Singh and Kaur, which tradition links to the founding of the Khalsa, in place of or alongside family surnames, and read ashtpadi nine of Sukhmani Sahib as a call to substance over status.

o: a title for a Sikh scholar or priest
lion, a name shared across every caste
a family name showing noble rank

p: where tradition says the names began
the title you can set down

s: every Sikh uses only Singh or Kaur as a surname
some do; others use them alongside a family name. there's real variety.
Singh and Kaur were given to everyone, whatever their caste
the same names for all, at the founding of the Khalsa.
ashtpadi nine says titles decide who someone is
the name is nothing without the substance underneath it.

games.q: you're known as 'the expert' at work. living ashtpadi nine, what do you try?
o: make sure everyone uses your title.
keep the knowledge, drop the badge, and help anyway.
games.why: substance over title: the work stays; the label goes; people know you by how you live.

practice: Name to yourself one title you quietly carry, the smart one, the fixer, the good one, the busy one, and imagine setting it down beside you like a heavy bag.
Breathe, and ask who you are without it; probably the same person, just lighter. If you pray, you can offer your good deeds without your name on them.

wordCard.voice: Singh, lion. The name given at the Khalsa's founding, the same for everyone, whatever caste: drop one title, keep the substance.

carryVoice: Your line: substance over title. People know you best by how you live. Day four hundred seventy-three, done.
